## Appendix A Derivation of Hartree and Fock energies for RMG spinors

We evaluate the Hartree and Fock energies Eqs. (20,21) explicitly. Recall that the spinor is given by

$$ \chi^{(N_{L})}_{n+1}\coloneqq\chi^{(N_{L})}(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{n+1})=\mathcal{N}(1,\eta e^{2\pi in/6},\eta^{2}e^{4\pi in/6},\ldots,\eta^{N_{L}-1}e^{2\pi i(N_{L}-1)n/6}), $$

where $\mathcal{N}=1/\sqrt{\sum_{a=0}^{N_{L}-1}\eta^{2a}}$ .

The form factor is defined by $\Lambda_{n,m}=\chi^{\dagger}_{n}\chi_{m}$ . Then,

$$ \displaystyle\Lambda_{3,1} \displaystyle=\Lambda_{6,4}=\mathcal{N}^{2}\sum_{n=0}^{N_{L}-1}\eta^{2n}e^{-2\pi in/3}, \displaystyle\Lambda_{1,2} \displaystyle=\Lambda_{4,5}=\mathcal{N}^{2}\sum_{n=0}^{N_{L}-1}\eta^{2n}e^{2\pi in/6}. $$

Therefore, we get

$$ \displaystyle\epsilon_{H}(C) \displaystyle=\frac{2}{3}\mathrm{Re}[e^{2\pi iC/3}\Lambda_{1,3}\Lambda_{4,6}] \displaystyle=\frac{2}{3}\mathrm{Re}\left[e^{2\pi iC/3}\left(\mathcal{N}^{2}\sum_{n=0}^{N_{L}-1}\eta^{2n}e^{2\pi in/3}\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle=\frac{2}{3}\mathcal{N}^{4}\sum_{a,b=0}^{N_{L}-1}\eta^{2(a+b)}\mathrm{Re}[e^{2\pi iC/3}e^{i2(a+b)\phi}] \displaystyle=\frac{2}{3}\mathcal{N}^{4}\sum_{a,b=0}^{N_{L}-1}\eta^{2(a+b)}\cos\left(\frac{2\pi(a+b+C)}{3}\right) $$

Similarly, we get for Fock

$$ \displaystyle\epsilon_{F}(C) \displaystyle=-\frac{2}{3}\mathrm{Re}[e^{-2\pi iC/3}\Lambda_{1,2}\Lambda_{4,5}] \displaystyle=-\frac{2}{3}\mathrm{Re}\left[e^{-2\pi iC/3}\left(\mathcal{N}^{2}\sum_{n=0}^{N_{L}-1}\eta^{2n}e^{2\pi in/3}\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle=-\frac{2}{3}\mathcal{N}^{4}\sum_{a,b=0}^{N_{L}-1}\eta^{2(a+b)}\mathrm{Re}[e^{-2\pi iC/3}e^{2\pi i(a+b)/3}] \displaystyle=-\frac{2}{3}\mathcal{N}^{4}\sum_{a,b=0}^{N_{L}-1}\eta^{2(a+b)}\cos\left(\frac{2\pi(a+b-2C)}{6}\right) $$

## Appendix B Proof of degeneracy under contact interaction

We will now prove the curious fact that if $\kappa$ and $\kappa^{\prime}$ spinors only have two components (with angular momentum $0$ and $1$ , respectively), then the Chern number $0$ and $1$ states will remain degenerate under contact interaction.

We now define

$$ \chi(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{1})=\begin{pmatrix}a_{\kappa}\\
b_{\kappa}\end{pmatrix},\quad\chi(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{4})=\begin{pmatrix}a_{\kappa^{\prime}}\\
b_{\kappa^{\prime}}\end{pmatrix}. $$

The $C_{3}$ action is given again by $\hat{C}_{3}=\mathrm{diag}(1,e^{2\pi i/3})$ . We fix the gauge such that $\chi(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{j+2})=\hat{C}_{3}\chi(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{j})$ .

Making use of Eqs. (15,16), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\epsilon_{H}(C) \displaystyle=\frac{2}{3}\mathrm{Re}\left[e^{2\pi iC/3}\Lambda_{1,3}\Lambda_{4,6}\right] \displaystyle=\frac{2}{3}\mathrm{Re}\left[e^{2\pi iC/3}(|a_{\kappa}|^{2}+e^{2\pi i/3}|b_{\kappa}|^{2})(|a_{\kappa^{\prime}}|^{2}+e^{2\pi i/3}|b_{\kappa^{\prime}}|^{2})\right] \displaystyle=\frac{2}{3}\left(|a_{\kappa}|^{2}|a_{\kappa^{\prime}}|^{2}\cos(2\pi C/3)+(|a_{\kappa}|^{2}|b_{\kappa^{\prime}}|^{2}+|b_{\kappa}|^{2}|a_{\kappa^{\prime}}|^{2})\cos(2\pi(C+1)/3)+|b_{\kappa}|^{2}|b_{\kappa^{\prime}}|^{2}\cos(2\pi(C+2)/3)\right), $$

$$ \displaystyle\epsilon_{F}(C) \displaystyle=-\frac{2}{3}\mathrm{Re}\left[e^{-2\pi iC/3}\Lambda_{1,2}\Lambda_{4,5}\right] \displaystyle=-\frac{2}{3}\mathrm{Re}\left[e^{-2\pi iC/3}(\overline{a_{\kappa}}a_{\kappa^{\prime}}+e^{-2\pi i/3}\overline{b_{\kappa}}b_{\kappa^{\prime}})(\overline{a_{\kappa^{\prime}}}a_{\kappa}+e^{-2\pi i/3}\overline{b_{\kappa^{\prime}}}b_{\kappa})\right] \displaystyle=-\frac{2}{3}\left(|a_{\kappa}|^{2}|a_{\kappa^{\prime}}|^{2}\cos(2\pi C/3)+(\overline{a_{\kappa^{\prime}}}a_{\kappa}\overline{b_{\kappa}}b_{\kappa^{\prime}}+\overline{a_{\kappa}}a_{\kappa^{\prime}}\overline{b_{\kappa^{\prime}}}b_{\kappa})\cos(2\pi(C+1)/3)+|b_{\kappa}|^{2}|b_{\kappa^{\prime}}|^{2}\cos(2\pi(C+2)/3)\right) $$

In contact interactions, we can take $V_{\boldsymbol{g}}=V_{\kappa}=1$ . Thus

$$ \displaystyle E(C) \displaystyle=\epsilon_{H}(C)+\epsilon_{F}(C)=\frac{2}{3}\cos\left(\frac{2\pi(C+1)}{3}\right)|\overline{a_{\kappa}}a_{\kappa^{\prime}}-\overline{b_{\kappa}}b_{\kappa^{\prime}}|^{2} $$

which means that $E(0)=E(1)$ . We note that contact interaction annihilates all intra-orbital interactions, and one can generally prove that the $C=0$ and $C=1$ states are still degenerate under any inter-orbital interaction.

## Appendix C Real space properties of orbitals at $\kappa$ and $\kappa^{\prime}$

*Figure 10: Real-space plot of high-symmetry point wavefunctions $\phi_{\tau,\ell_{\mathrm{tot}}}(\boldsymbol{r})$ . The size of the circles corresponds to the amplitudes of the wavefunctions at the Wyckoff points, and the color corresponds to the phase of the wavefunctions. The rows correspond to different high symmetry points (a) $\kappa$ and (b) $\kappa^{\prime}$ , and the columns correspond to different angular momenta $\ell_{\mathrm{tot}}$ . Different wavefunctions at the same high-symmetry point are related by translations.*

In this appendix, we will explain two elementary characteristics of $C_{3}$ symmetric orbitals at $\kappa$ and $\kappa^{\prime}$ points. Recall that Wyckoff positions are points in the unit cell that are invariant under a spatial symmetry action. With the current choice of the lattice, these points are integer multiples of

$$ \tilde{\boldsymbol{a}}=\frac{1}{3}(\boldsymbol{a}_{1}+\boldsymbol{a}_{2}). $$

Below we will establish the following two facts:

- 1. The orbital-resolved charge densities of $C_{3}$ symmetric states at $\kappa$ and $\kappa^{\prime}$ points have peaks and zeros at the Wyckoff points, determined by both the orbital angular momentum $\ell_{a}$ and the state angular momentum $\ell_{\xi}$ ;

- 2. The action of the translation $T_{\tilde{\boldsymbol{a}}}$ translates $\ell_{\kappa}\to\ell_{\kappa}+1$ , and $\ell_{\kappa^{\prime}}\to\ell_{\kappa^{\prime}}-1$ .

To understand the first statement, take the $\boldsymbol{\kappa}$ point without loss of generality. Now, consider the state $\psi_{\kappa,\ell_{\kappa}}(\boldsymbol{r})$ : its orbital-resolved charge density is given by

$$ \rho_{\kappa}^{a}(\boldsymbol{r},\ell_{\kappa})=\left|\psi^{a}_{\kappa,\ell_{\kappa}}(\boldsymbol{r})\right|^{2}. $$

We now make use of the definition Eq. (5). Consider the momentum point $\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{1}$ : Let’s say $\chi^{a}(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{1})=\chi_{0}$ . Then, due to the gauge choice $\chi(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{3})=\hat{C}_{3}\chi(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{1})$ , we have $\chi^{a}(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{3})=\exp[2\pi i\ell_{a}/3]\chi_{0}$ , and similarly $\chi^{a}(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{5})=\exp[4\pi i\ell_{a}/3]\chi_{0}$ .

We may now compute the angular-momentum resolved charge density:

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{\kappa}^{\ell_{a}}(\boldsymbol{r},\ell_{\kappa}) \displaystyle=\left|\psi^{a}_{\kappa,\ell_{\kappa}}(\boldsymbol{r})\right|^{2} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{3}\left|\sum_{j=1,3,5}\exp{\left[\frac{2\pi i\ell_{\kappa}}{3}\frac{j}{2}\right]}e^{i\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{j}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}\chi(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{j})^{a}\right|^{2} \displaystyle=\frac{\left|\chi(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{1})^{a}\right|^{2}}{3}\left|\sum_{j=1,3,5}\exp{\left[\frac{2\pi i(\ell_{a}+\ell_{\kappa})}{3}\frac{j}{2}\right]}e^{i\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{j}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}\right| \displaystyle=\left|\chi(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{1})^{a}\right|^{2}\left|\varphi_{\kappa,\ell_{\kappa}+\ell_{a}}(\boldsymbol{r})\right|^{2} $$

Since $\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{j}\cdot\tilde{\boldsymbol{a}}=2\pi j/3$ for $j\in 1,3,5$ and $-2\pi j/3$ for $j=2,4,6$ (modulo $2\pi$ ), we may immediately deduce

$$ \rho_{\kappa}^{a}(m\tilde{\boldsymbol{a}},\ell_{\kappa})=3\left|\chi(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{1})^{a}\right|^{2}\delta_{m,\ell_{a}+\ell_{\kappa}}. $$

where the $\delta_{m,n}=1$ if $3|(m-n)$ and $0$ otherwise.

This motivates a definition of

$$ \ell_{\mathrm{tot}}=\ell_{a}+\ell_{\kappa}. $$

Indeed, a similar calculation for the $\kappa^{\prime}$ shows that

$$ \rho_{\tau}^{a}(m\tilde{\boldsymbol{a}},\ell_{\tau})\propto\delta_{m,\tau\ell_{\mathrm{tot}}}. $$

where $\tau=\pm$ labels the $\kappa$ and $\kappa^{\prime}$ points.

This establishes the first fact: the peak of the charge density is at a Wyckoff position determined by a signed total angular momentum, $\tau(\ell_{a}+\ell_{\tau})$ . Particularly, one can see in Fig. 10 that although the charge density peaks of $\ell_{\mathrm{tot}}=1$ at $\kappa$ point and $\ell_{\mathrm{tot}}=-1$ at $\kappa^{\prime}$ point share the same Wyckoff positions, the wavefunctions have different phase structures and thus different angular momenta.

As for the second fact, we show it explicitly:

$$ \displaystyle(T_{\tilde{\boldsymbol{a}}}\psi_{\kappa})(\boldsymbol{r},\ell_{\kappa}) \displaystyle=\psi_{\kappa}(\boldsymbol{r}-\tilde{\boldsymbol{a}},\ell_{\kappa}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sum_{j=1,3,5}\exp{\left[\frac{2\pi i\ell_{\kappa}}{3}\frac{j}{2}\right]}e^{i\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{j}\cdot(\boldsymbol{r}-\tilde{\boldsymbol{a}})}\chi(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{j}) \displaystyle\propto\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sum_{j=1,3,5}\exp{\left[\frac{2\pi i(\ell_{\kappa}+1)}{3}\frac{j}{2}\right]}e^{i\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{j}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}\chi(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{j}) \displaystyle=\psi_{\kappa}(\boldsymbol{r},\ell_{\kappa}+1). $$

The $\kappa^{\prime}$ point calculation is exactly similar. Both of these statements can be checked graphically in Fig. 10.

## Appendix D Justification of the three-patch model

In this appendix, we will motivate the building blocks of the three-patch model from simple physical conditions of the single-particle band structure. We will also discuss how we arrive at the restricted Hilbert space in Eq. (5) and below.

Spontaneous translation symmetry breaking can occur in the case that the interaction strength $U$ is much larger than the bandwidth of the lowest band within the mBZ:

$$ |E({\boldsymbol{\gamma}})-E({\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{i}})|\lesssim U $$

In the limit where the lowest band is completely flat, the Fermi surface can be arbitrarily deformed without being penalized by the kinetic energy. In this way, we can create low-energy Fermi surfaces with perfect nesting conditions, which are in general unstable to the creation of insulating states by the exchange interaction. This thus corresponds to condition (i) stated at the beginning of Sec. II. Once we take the dispersion into account, a gap equation must be solved to investigate the existence of such instabilities, which is performed under various approximations in Sec. III.6.

The “weak coupling mean field” assumption has two subparts. It firstly states that the state is weakly coupled. This can also be implemented by an energetic constraint: we need a large gap between the $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ point and its higher harmonics, which means that there will be a large direct gap around the $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ point in the folded band structure. In the case where

$$ E(\boldsymbol{\gamma}+\boldsymbol{g}_{i})-E(\boldsymbol{\gamma})>U, $$

interactions cannot hybridize the $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ point wavefunction with other plane waves, and thus the state will be weakly coupled. It also states that the state can be described as a Slater determinant state. While this mean-field approximation is uncontrolled, as long as we consider a variational space of Hartree-Fock states, this assumption is always satisfied.

The three-patch assumption is harder to justify a priori from the knowledge of the single-particle Hamiltonian $\hat{h}$ alone. Physically, the Fock interaction is strong between nearby momentum given the small momentum exchange, and thus the single particle wavefunctions can be plausibly inferred to be similar. However, realistically, the best we can do is an a posteriori justification by inspecting the nature of the SCHF ground state, which we have performed carefully for the ground states of the RMG Hamiltonian.

In the remainder of this section, we will explain in detail how to physically obtain the reduced Hilbert space Eq. (5) from the assumptions above.

We only consider Slater determinant states. After we fold the Brillouin zone, the states are then labeled by crystalline momentum $\boldsymbol{k}$ :

$$ \ket{\Psi}=\prod_{\boldsymbol{k}}\prod_{j=1}^{n_{\boldsymbol{k}}}d^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k},j}\ket{0}, $$

where $n_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ is the occupation number at mBZ momentum $\boldsymbol{k}$ , and $d^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k},j}$ is the creation operator with mBZ momentum $\boldsymbol{k}$ . Since we assumed the state to be an insulator, we fill the low-energy band of the mean-field Hamiltonian in the mBZ such that $n_{\boldsymbol{k}}=1$ for all crystalline momentum $\boldsymbol{k}$ .

The weak-coupling assumption then allows us to reduce to a low-energy Hilbert space with the lowest energy plane waves. Explicitly, we can restrict to a Slater determinant states generated by low energy plane waves:

$$ \hat{d}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}n}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{g}}\psi^{\boldsymbol{g}}_{\boldsymbol{k}n}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{g}}. $$

Here the sum over $\boldsymbol{g}$ is only non-zero when $E(\boldsymbol{k}+\boldsymbol{g})-E(\boldsymbol{k})$ is small relative to the interaction strength.

Finally, the three-patch enables a further reduction to an analytically tractable model. Since the wavefunction is assumed to be homogeneous within each patch, we pick one representative momentum to describe the whole patch. The most natural choice is the set of high symmetry points $\xi=\left\{{\gamma},{\kappa},{\kappa}^{\prime}\right\}$ . Schematically, this reduction in Hilbert space can be written as:

$$ \ket{\Psi}=\prod_{\boldsymbol{k}\in\mathrm{mBZ}}d^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{0}\xrightarrow[\text{transformation}]{\text{three-patch}}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}\boldsymbol{k}\in\\
\{\gamma,\kappa,\kappa^{\prime}\}\end{subarray}}d^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\ket{0}=\ket{\Psi_{\mathrm{3p}}} $$

The high symmetry points $\left\{{\gamma},{\kappa},{\kappa}^{\prime}\right\}$ have one, three, and three low-energy states respectively. We will assume that electronic states from the higher shells have a gap to these low-energy states that is much larger compared to the interaction energy. Following (79), and $C_{3}$ symmetry, the associated creation operators are $\hat{d}^{\dagger}_{{\gamma}},\hat{d}^{\dagger}_{{\kappa},\ell_{{\kappa}}}$ , and $\hat{d}^{\dagger}_{{\kappa}^{\prime},\ell_{{\kappa}^{\prime}}}$ with $C_{3}$ angular momentum $\ell_{\xi}$ . Their single-particle wavefunctions $\psi(\boldsymbol{r})=\braket{\boldsymbol{r}|\hat{d}^{\dagger}|0}$ are thus given by Eq. (5), which we reproduce here

$$ \displaystyle\psi_{\gamma,\ell_{\gamma}=0} \displaystyle=\chi(\gamma) \displaystyle\psi_{\kappa,\ell_{\kappa}}(\boldsymbol{r}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sum_{j=1,3,5}\exp{\left[\frac{2\pi i\ell_{\kappa}}{3}\frac{j}{2}\right]}e^{i\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{j}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}\chi(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{j}), \displaystyle\psi_{\kappa^{\prime},\ell_{\kappa^{\prime}}}(\boldsymbol{r}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sum_{j=2,4,6}\exp{\left[\frac{2\pi i\ell_{\kappa^{\prime}}}{3}\frac{j}{2}\right]}e^{i\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{j}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}\chi(\boldsymbol{\kappa}_{j}). $$

By the assumption that we have an insulating state with $\nu=1$ , we have one electron per representative state in the patch. Together with the Slater determinant assumption, we arrive at variational states

$$ \Psi_{\ell_{{\kappa}},\ell_{{\kappa}^{\prime}}}(\boldsymbol{r}_{1},\boldsymbol{r}_{2},\boldsymbol{r}_{3})=\mathcal{A}[\psi_{\gamma}(\boldsymbol{r}_{1}),\psi_{\kappa,\ell_{\kappa}}(\boldsymbol{r}_{2}),\psi_{\kappa^{\prime},\ell_{\boldsymbol{\kappa}^{\prime}}}(\boldsymbol{r}_{3})]. $$

This establishes the three-patch model.

We now use the charge density pattern above to infer some features of the Hartree and Fock energies. The Hartree energy between $\psi_{\kappa}$ and $\psi_{\kappa^{\prime}}$ corresponds to the interaction energy of classical charge configurations. It now becomes a simple visual exercise: we can visually figure out which charge densities are on top of each other by looking at Fig. 11. At small $\eta$ , the Fock term can be similarly graphically evaluated. This is because Fock exchange energy is controlled by the alignment of pseudospins, and at small $\eta$ most weight is on the top layer. We conclude the $C=0$ state has the lowest Fock energy due to the large overlap between the top layer charge densities, as confirmed in the Fock energy plot in Fig. 11. We note, however, that this visual exercise misses other contributions such as intercomponent interactions, and is qualitatively incorrect at large $\eta$ , as evidenced by the fact that $C=1$ state can have lower Fock energy.

We note an interesting implication of the density patterns. Consider a potential such that $V(\boldsymbol{r})=V_{0}\sum_{i}\cos(\boldsymbol{g}_{i}\cdot\boldsymbol{r})$ , where $V_{0}<0$ . This potential has a honeycomb shape, where the electrons are favored to form a triangular lattice at the superlattice points. If we apply this potential to the first component of the spinor, the $C=0$ state, which has a triangular charge density in the first component, gains more energy than $C=\pm 1$ states. On the other hand, if the potential is applied to the second component, the $C=1$ state is favored over the other states, since the charge density of the second component forms a triangular lattice. This consideration implies that the phase boundary can be shifted by such external potentials.
